items.title: 2027 Lamborghini Temerario Spyder: 10,250 RPM With the Top Down
items.summary:
How do you make an already-wicked Italian supercar that revs to 10,000 RPM even better? Easy: take the roof off and give it, uh, an even higher redline. That’s what’s up with the new 2027 Lamborghini Temerario Spyder. It keeps all the savage goodness of the “regular” Temerario, but it raises the RPM limit to 10,250 and loses the top so you can hear it better.

Of course, it doesn’t just lose its top. It merely hides it via a fully retractable hardtop, a first for Lambo in this category. Previously, they’ve been all soft tops. Per the automaker, the roof system utilizes 10 electric actuators to lower and raise the roof quickly and quietly, storing it vertically behind the seats, which is how Lamborghini was able to retain the see-through engine cover in the Spyder.

Lamborghini 

With the top down, the center of gravity drops by 3 mm compared with the closed configuration, while its longitudinal position remains practically identical and the car’s distribution is unaltered. This means the roadster’s dynamics remain just as pristine as the coupe. Per Lambo, a traditional roof setup that stashes away horizontally would’ve raised the center of gravity by approximately 7 mm and shifted it 11 mm towards the rear axle.

The mighty 4.0-liter twin-turbo V8 with three axial-flux electric motors remains, along with its 907 horsepower, 118 of which comes from the electric bits. The eight-speed dual-clutch transmission lets it launch from 0-60 mph in 2.8 seconds thanks to its electrified all-wheel drive, and reach a top speed of 213 mph. Bonus points if you reach that speed with the…
items.t: 2027 Lamborghini Temerario Spyder: 10,250 RPM With the Top Down

items.title: This 840-HP Eleanor Mustang Tribute Is a 2026 Underneath Its ’67-Style Skin
items.summary:
Today’s muscle cars are objectively better at going fast than their predecessors. That doesn’t mean they’re better, period. Some folks can’t help but want the drivability of a new V8 speed machine with the look of an old one. Vintage Modern makes vehicles for those people, and this S650 Ford Mustang with a carbon fiber Eleanor lookalike body is the latest. I personally can’t make heads or tails of it.

Everything sounds good on paper, for sure. It’s a brand new Mustang at its core, rocking either a stock 5.0-liter Coyote with 486 horsepower and 418 lb-ft of torque or a tuned version with a 3.0-liter Whipple supercharger making 850 hp and 615 lb-ft. I’d be lying if I said that doesn’t sound like a good time. 

And I’m not sure you could do any better with the bodywork, given the parameters. It’s least offensive from the front three-quarter view, when you crouch down low and can’t quite see the rounded roofline. That’s what throws everything off for me. The front looks alright on its own, with all that billet aluminum and the hood that juts out over the front bumper. But the back half isn’t great—at least, not from the side—as the fenders keep going for a mile beyond the rear wheels.

Vintage Modern 

I recognize that I’m not the intended customer for this car. I’d rather have an original 1967 Mustang fastback, one that’s slower and more cumbersome to live with. But I don’t have the money for either of them, so I guess I’ll leave my criticism at that.

For its part, Vintage Modern put a ton of work into this project, and it’s even crash-testing it. The boutique manufacturer…
items.t: This 840-HP Eleanor Mustang Tribute Is a 2026 Underneath Its ’67-Style Skin

The cars it will build in its new Georgia plant will be unibody SUVs like the Q7, Q8, and Q9. But America runs on trucks and SUVs, and the luxury division of Volkswagen Group is desperate to get into the body-on-frame SUV game with those healthy profit margins. Scout could be the answer.

You can listen below to Keogh address putting another topper on the Scout platform and building something for another Volkswagen Group brand at the automaker’s new factory.

“I would use the word capable,” Keogh said initially.

Keogh expanded by saying, “Yes. The platform is 100% capable of putting, let’s say, another brand hat on it, without a doubt. The factory is capable of doing that. The trans itself is a Tremec unit, but it was a tuner shop in Texas called Peitz Performance Tunes that actually cracked the code to make it functional. I caught up with Alex Peitz, the owner and tuner there, to find out how he worked his magic and when consumers will be able to buy their own C8 manual conversion kits.

First, I asked him what the car’s like to drive. And even though we have Hurd’s impressions (linked above), Peitz has a lot more miles on it, including highway blasts and running full noise on track.

What The C8 Manual’s Like To Drive 

“Like I tell everybody, it’s a transformative experience. It’s impossible to drive this car and not have a smile on your face. Actually, the president of Shelby American drove it on Sunday. He had a sneak peek into it and he was doing donuts in the parking lot of Shelby, and he loved it. I mean, you can just see his reaction.”

items.title: VW Dealers Are Suing Scout. Its CEO Is Invoking the Consitution
items.summary:
Scout Motors is part of Volkswagen Group thanks to the German automaker acquiring the rights when it bought Navistar in 2021, but the “startup” automaker is adamant it is its own company. To that point, it plans to go the direct sales route when it starts delivering vehicles in 2028. Naturally, Volkswagen and Audi dealerships are irate and suing .

On the latest episode of The Drivecast , Scout Motors President and CEO Scott Keogh exclusively told The Drive , “There is only plan A, and plan A is to execute it direct to consumer, ” when asked what Scout’s plan B if the direct sales route doesn’t work out. Keogh also argued that interstate commerce is protected by the Constitution, and that no judge can tell a consumer they can’t buy a Scout.

You can listen to Keogh address Scout going the direct sales route and the reasons why below.

“There is only plan A, and plan A is to execute it direct to consumer. And the reason there’s no plan B in my mind is, one, it’s strategically right,” Keogh said. 

Addressing why the direct sales route is strategically right, Keogh said, “In this environment, you wanna have a relationship directly with the customer. You wanna have direct control of the data. And in the world of AI, I promise you, you wanna have to do that. When you have someone’s agent buying a car from another person’s agent, spiraled across thousands of dealerships, it’s, it’s gonna be chaos . So 100% is the right strategy.”

Keogh went so far as to address the law and its limits, particularly around commerce. “If you look at it, if you wanna look at it the other way, a…

items.title: This School Bus Was Repurposed Into the Ultimate Hay Mover—And It Runs Backwards
items.summary:
There are a lot of fantastic tools out there, and I’m convinced some of the best are those you build yourself . If you have a super specific job to do, it’s not a bad idea to forge or fabricate an arsenal of super specialized equipment to get it done. I feel like Dallas Henry would agree, as he has done it time and again—perhaps most notably with a 25-year-old school bus that now operates as a hay loader .

It’s a 2001 International 3800 with a venerable DT466 diesel engine. And while that compression-ignition lump is still under the hood, it isn’t at the front of the loader bus; it’s at the back. That’s because Henry flipped its orientation around so that the ring gear is on the opposite side of the pinion gear, reversing the drive direction. The Allison automatic and auxiliary transmission retain all of their forward gears; the machine simply drives the other way.

“If all tie rods and steering components are right, it works real good,” Henry told me. “Top speed was 36 mph. I recently put a newer rear end that accepts the hub pilot wheels. The gear ratio is a little lower. Haven’t had it on the road to tell. I usually haul it at distances.”

Dallas Henry 

In the field is where this rig really shines. The front-end loader is an Art’s Way 5000 unit built in the late ’60s or early ’70s, originally intended for articulated 4×4 tractors. Henry fabbed it to fit the bus instead, and now he has a machine that will lift as much as 9,000 pounds—more hay than he could realistically skewer with the forks. The hydraulics run off a 22-gallon-per-minute direct-drive gear pump, and the…
items.t: This School Bus Was Repurposed Into the Ultimate Hay Mover—And It Runs Backwards

items.title: $59K. No Removable Doors. An IPO? Scout’s CEO Just Told Us What’s Real
items.summary:
Two years ago Volkswagen Group revived Scout from the grave, showed off some pretty rad concept cars with some pretty tantalizing specs , and a pretty enticing price. A lot’s changed in the world, and healthy skepticism is only natural when it comes to reviving an iconic automaker.

Now validation units are moving off the assembly line in a 90% completed factory. On the latest episode of The Drivecast , Scout Motors President and CEO Scott Keogh sat down exclusively with The Drive to sort fact from fiction, talk pricing, timing, the competition, and reality.

Keogh’s mission is no easy feat, bringing an American icon back from the graveyard as an EV, making it relevant to generations of people who weren’t even born yet when the last Scout was built in 1980, and developing a complex battery electric platform with a gas engine range extender.

Not to mention, doing all of that under the Volkswagen Group, which got the rights to Scout with its acquisition of heavy-duty truck manufacturer Navistar in 2021. It’s got plenty of other problems right now as sales in China are flatlining and its other EV efforts are struggling, but the reason it’s poured billions into resurrecting Scout is because the Germans know America doesn’t run on Dunkin. It runs on trucks. VW Group doesn’t have any body-on-frame pickups or SUVs for sale in this country, which means it’s missing out on a huge profit center. It sees Scout as critical for getting its finances back on track. Scout revealed its first pickup in SUV concepts in 2024, which somehow was two years ago, and they looked amazing. Too good…
items.t: $59K. No Removable Doors. An IPO? Scout’s CEO Just Told Us What’s Real

items.title: I Can’t Stop Looking at This Unholy BMW E39 With an OBS Ford F-150 Body Swap
items.summary:
Many folks are into engine swaps, but there’s a special subgroup of enthusiasts who love to use their talents… differently. How, exactly? Allow me to point you toward this: A BMW E39 with none other than a Ford F-150 body swap.

This lovely-looking Frankenstein’s monster of sorts belongs to New York-based bespoke car builder, Hofmeister Haus . Judging from the shop’s Instagram account and website, this oddball creation is one of the many BMW-related builds it’s put out over time—and frankly, they all look pretty darn good. At least in the photos and videos.

View this post on Instagram 

According to a post by Tarık Şimşek in the Facebook group Unibody Chassis and Body Swaps , the entire “OBS Ford over E39 BMW” project was completed in just three days—or so I gather from the phrase “another 3 day swap.” That’s not a whole lot of time to perform such a complex operation, but then again, it looks like Şimşek and the Hofmeister Haus team have done it before.

“Swap went extremely well and all systems functional,” the Facebook post reads. “We need to weigh it, but assuming the end weight is about exactly as it was in BMW form. Quite surprised it held up fine at highway speeds with zero flex lol. Gonna be cutting the strut brace/rear wall after making sure we weld all necessary reinforcements. That way, the bed area is usable like an actual pickup truck.”

Watching the videos above is borderline unsettling. From the outside, the truck looks like any other dropped and chopped-up pickup, until the camera peeks into the cabin. Then, boom! It’s a BMW! And not just any BMW, but an…
items.t: I Can’t Stop Looking at This Unholy BMW E39 With an OBS Ford F-150 Body Swap

items.title: We Drove a Manual Chevy Corvette C8, and It’s Exactly What America’s Sports Car Needs
items.summary:
The Chevrolet Corvette C8 was a big pivot for the Bowtie. It wasn’t just the first Corvette with the engine behind the driver; it was also the first to offer a dual-clutch automatic transmission—and only a dual-clutch automatic transmission. After decades of front-engine development, Chevy faced the daunting cost of building a pair of new transaxles (one manual, one automatic) that could mate with a mid-engine car.

Needless to say, developing two gearboxes wasn’t (and still isn’t) in GM’s budget . Now, I wasn’t in the room, and I can’t say exactly how that all played out (and those who were won’t say), but the smart money says that when faced with the choice between either pleasing a vanishingly small group of enthusiasts and winning comparison tests against far more expensive equipment, executives simply chose the latter.

A marketing decision, one might argue, but one that produced a particularly excellent and very capable Corvette. But many of us would still gladly give up a few tenths in the quarter-mile or lap time for the simple enjoyment of operating a manual.

Andrew Collins 

Enter Tremec, the company that built America’s most beloved six-speed gearbox —the transmission employed in GM’s own performance cars, including both Blackwings (RIP CT4) and the also-departed Camaro. And despite rumors to the contrary, its manual C8 development car is quite real . How do I know? Well, I just drove it.

Tremec invited me (along with several potential customers) to sample its whole suite of transmissions at a new (so much so that it’s not on Google yet), private track outside…
items.t: We Drove a Manual Chevy Corvette C8, and It’s Exactly What America’s Sports Car Needs

items.title: Off-Road Guru Develops Budget Portal Axle by Flipping His Jeep’s Rear Diff Upside Down
items.summary:
Portal axles can be a hardcore four-wheeler’s best friend. They instantly elevate a truck, and I’m not just talking about its ride height. I’m talking about its ability to conquer obstacles, whether we’re talking Moab slickrock or Icelandic volcanoes. But there’s one problem: They’re obscenely expensive. That’s what makes this portal axle build by Zeph Gage so interesting. Well, that, and the fact that he’s only installing one on the rear of his Jeep.

Before we go any further, give me a second to explain what portal axles are for anyone unfamiliar. And you know what—actually, allow me to pass the mic to my coworker Andrew Collins , who wrote a stellar story about driving portal-axle Ineos Grenadiers through the Arctic :

“Portal axles are conceptually simple but practically spectacular pieces of engineering that make the vehicle running them much taller than a traditional drivetrain allows. Instead of shafts and other components hanging down from the transmission and transfer case, portal axles put a stack of gears behind each driven wheel.

“That setup lets the axle shafts be tucked up real high, so there’s very little hardware hanging down below the truck’s frame line. Add tall tires (we ran 37-inch BF Goodrich KM3 mud terrains), and you can make enough room to have a picnic under the vehicle while it’s parked.”

My amigo Andrew did a great job assembling some visual assets to help explain how portal axles work. And just look at the difference between a solid-axle Grenadier and one with portals! Andrew Collins 

Typically, a set of portal axles from companies like…
items.t: Off-Road Guru Develops Budget Portal Axle by Flipping His Jeep’s Rear Diff Upside Down

items.title: Man Drives U-Haul Box Truck 1,200 Miles To Get Home During Nationwide Ground Stop
items.summary:
Last week’s nationwide ground stop threw a heap of chaos into one of the busiest travel seasons of the year, but that wasn’t going to stop Greg Swan from getting home from Dallas to Minneapolis. With all flights canceled, no rental cars available, and no viable train route, Swan grabbed a one-way Chevy Express rental from U-Haul and drove that sucker 1,200 miles home. Where have we seen this before ?

If you think about it, it does make sense; U-Haul’s business is optimized for one-way rentals, after all. And I’m sure most of the nation’s travelers marooned by the FAA’s nationwide ground stop would not think to do that in their desperation to get where they were going.

“It was my Muse AI agent’s idea!” Swan told us. “No flights, rental cars, bus, or train options anywhere. Too much going on at home to play the rebook and cancellation game. But U-Haul had two one-way trucks to choose from! Long drive, but worth it to be home.”

Swan also shared some choice driving impressions. “Also, no cruise control. And a speed governor that wouldn’t let it go faster than 73 mph. And a super strong spring in that accelerator for pushing down on it for 21 hours. My calf is pissed. Belt screaming down the interstate. A miserable driving experience.”

“After 21 hours on the road, Swan dropped his colleague off at the Minneapolis airport at 3:15 a.m. Sunday, before Swan arrived home at 4 a.m.,” News 9 shared.

Greg Swan/X 

Having crossed the country in those box trucks a time or two myself, I say they ain’t that bad! But having to unexpectedly spend three days driving one when you thought…
items.t: Canceled Flight? Try U-Haul. One Desperate Traveller Went 1,200 Miles in an Empty Moving Truck Just To Get Home

items.title: The Aston Martin Dreadnought Is Going Racing for Real, but It Was Born From Call of Duty
items.summary:
Aston Martin is venturing into the exciting world of off-road rally racing , and it’s doing so with a sweet-looking truck: the Aston Martin Dreadnought. Originally conceived as a digital creation for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 , the Dreadnought is jumping into the mortal realm to do some serious racing at the 2027 Dakar rally .

This explains why when I first saw these photos on social media, I thought they were merely digital renderings or, as automakers like to call them nowadays, “creative exercises.” The off-roader was legit born as a video game war machine, yet it will go racing in the real world in a few months. Even better yet, Aston kept that steampunk-ness that makes it look like it doesn’t belong in reality. The stance, the bodywork, the livery—it’s all very cool and somewhat resembles a rally-fied Valiant.

Aston Martin 

No performance specs have been released yet, though it’s safe to assume the Dreadnought will not compete against its cross-town rival, the Defender, which races in the Stock class. It’ll most likely be powered by a V8 from the automaker’s stable, but that’s yet to be seen. Furthermore, Aston has chosen the racing experts at Prodrive as its engineering partner, greatly improving the brand’s odds of surviving its first-ever Dakar. 

Last but not least, Aston has hired some serious stars to get behind the wheel of its three machines. Performing driving duty will be two-time Formula 1 champion Fernando Alonso , nine-time World Rally Champion Sébastien Loeb, and reigning World Rally Raid Champion Lucas Moraes.

items.title: America’s Largest Car Exporter by Value Wants Tariff Relief: TDS
items.summary:
Good morning and welcome to The Downshift , a daily sweep of today’s top headlines from the auto industry and car culture, curated by The Drive’s editorial team. Each story gets a short summary and a link to the original source if you want to dive deeper.

Here’s what’s cooking on Tuesday, November 17, 2026:

BMW, like other automakers, is making a case to the Trump administration for tariff relief, based on a $1.7 billion investment in its South Carolina assembly plant, as well as its status as the U.S.’s largest automotive exporter by value. “Our business model is to export, so for sure we are in close contact with the federal government,” Robert Engelhorn, CEO of BMW Manufacturing, said in an interview. “We are looking towards free trade. We are looking toward the lower tariffs.” BMW paid the U.S. over $1 billion in import duties last year. [ Automotive News ] 

BMW is also betting big on its first U.S.-built EV, the iX5, though the vehicle is slightly more insulated from manufacturing and financial pitfalls than competing models, since it’s built on the same assembly line as versions with other powertrains, and also uses battery cells from an outside supplier rather than those constructed in-house. items.title: Toyota’s Scion KEI-01 First-Drive Review: A Billy Goat Many People Are Going to Want
items.summary:
Key Takeaways 

Toyota revives Scion with KEI-01. The right-hand-drive Kei truck is legally coming to America, targeting niche markets. 

Unique design and features. Compact size, removable bed sides, and right-hand drive make it stand out. 

Off-road capability shines. The KEI-01 climbs like a billy goat with its 660 cc engine and four-wheel drive. 

Competitive pricing potential. Expected to cost under $30,000, making it an attractive option for fleet buyers. 

Bottom line: Toyota's Scion KEI-01 is a quirky, capable Kei truck poised to capture a unique market with its off-road prowess and competitive pricing. 

✦ 
 AI assisted, editor reviewed 

As you may have heard, Toyota is bringing back Scion, and its first product will be a right-hand-drive Kei truck named KEI-01 . We don’t know much about the KEI-01, but we know what matters: it’s a Kei truck being brought legally to America.

A day after the reveal, I got to drive the KEI-01 on a gravel course to get an initial impression. Here’s what I learned in those few minutes:

A Kei truck is an ultra-compact, purposeful truck built to meet Japan’s keijidōsha (light vehicle) class. Strict size limits keep these things from being wider than 5 feet and no longer than just over 11 feet. They aren’t powerful, they aren’t fancy, and they’re usually extremely capable, especially given their size.

Joel Feder 

The outside looks like a miniature cabover truck you might see in the toy aisle at Target or like someone shrunk a European truck. It’s like nothing on the road here in the U.S. The cab is upright; there’s basically no…
items.t: Toyota’s Scion KEI-01 First-Drive Review: A Billy Goat Many People Are Going to Want

items.title: Toyota’s Scion KEI-01 Kei Truck Will Cost Less Than $30,000—And $22,000 ‘Seems Reasonable’
items.summary:
Last week, something borderline unbelievable happened: Toyota said it would sell a Kei truck in the U.S. market. Actually, two unbelievable things happened, as the automaker also said it would revive the Scion brand from the graveyard.

Questions abound, but from the outset it’s clear Toyota’s Scion KEI-01 truck will be a low-volume affair, at least for now. But what will it cost? Toyota USA’s Vice President of Engineering, Don Federico, told The Drive that “$22,000 seems reasonable” and “It’ll cost less than $30,000.”

As one of the few people who have driven Scion’s KEI-01, I can tell you it’s like a little billy goat, and so many people will want this thing. But maybe not you. No one’s going to be hauling their kid to school or soccer practice in this thing. For the money, a Ford Maverick makes a lot more sense.

But ranchers, hotels, municipalities, and so many other outfits, including small businesses, looking for a little workhorse might be lining up for this thing. Especially for that pricing.

Federico was quick to note it’s really not hard in this day and age to spend $30,000, $35,000, or (and I probably twisted my face when he told me this) up to $45,000 on a utility UTV featuring four-wheel drive, an enclosed cab with both air conditioning and heat, and a radio. What’s more, those more expensive machines don’t come with a bulletproof 660 cc three-cylinder engine, a factory warranty from Toyota, or the ability to be serviced at a Toyota dealership. They dot America like McDonald’s.

As someone who isn’t living in the world of UTVs and small utility vehicles, my…
items.t: Toyota’s Scion KEI-01 Kei Truck Will Cost Less Than $30,000—And $22,000 ‘Seems Reasonable’
